We live in a world where medical care begins at the disease. Most appointments are reserved for diagnosis, not for prevention. By the time the system pays attention, years of daily choices have already spoken.

🌿

Food is one of the most powerful things you do every single day, and one of the least intentional. Here, we place it at the centre of your health: not as a diet, not as a rule, but as the daily architecture of how you feel, how you age, and how you live.

✦

We do not eat as punishment. We do not skip, compensate, or restrict. We nourish. With knowledge, with beauty, and with the understanding that every meal is an act of care for the body you will live in for decades.

🕯

This is the space where you slow down. Where food becomes a reason to sit, to breathe, and to connect. With yourself first, and then with the people you love. The table is a relationship, not just a surface.

◉

Grounded in science, guided by experts

This is not a replacement for professional medical advice. It is a guide built on the clinical and scientific work of the people who have spent their careers studying how humans truly thrive.

Dr. Peter Attia Dr. Carlos Jaramillo Rafael Santandreu Dr. Robert Lustig

How to Practice
🕯

Practice this ritual with at least one of your meals. It doesn't need to be every meal, every day. The first three weeks are yours alone, solo, so the practice can anchor before life joins it. Choose the meal that fits your rhythm: the quiet dinner, the unhurried lunch, the slow breakfast before the day starts. Habit is built in repetition, not in perfection.

Rituals are designed to start on the 1st of each month. Choose the month you want to begin. If you subscribed during the first days of the month, start the ritual right away. If you subscribed after the 3rd, we recommend starting the following month so you can complete the full 30-day journey.

The Marmaroph Plate · Feng Shui Balance

In feng shui, food is medicine through color. Each color nourishes a different element and organ system. Your plate should have at least 3 colors at every meal.

The ancient Chinese understood that a balanced plate mirrors a balanced body. When you eat all five colors daily, you feed every major organ system — liver, heart, stomach, lungs, and kidneys. This is not decoration. This is functional nutrition through color.

The Marmaroph Plate — Every Meal, Every Day

¼ protein · ¼ whole grain · ½ vegetables (3+ colors) · 1 tbsp healthy fat

These proportions reduce inflammation, stabilize blood sugar, and keep you full for 4-5 hours. No calorie counting needed — just follow the plate.

Your anchor object

Habit Liberation

Free yourself gently

The food drugs you don’t know about

Some of the most addictive substances on Earth are not sold by dealers — they are sold in supermarkets, offered at parties, and normalised by culture. They hijack the same dopamine reward system in your brain as cocaine, nicotine, and heroin. The difference? Society tells you they are fine. They are not.

🍬Sugar

Sugar is a dopamine drug — pharmacologically identical in mechanism to alcohol and nicotine. It activates the mesolimbic reward pathway in the nucleus accumbens, creating tolerance (you need more), withdrawal (headaches, irritability), and compulsive use despite harm. Dr. Robert Lustig at UCSF has demonstrated that fructose is metabolised by the liver in the same pathway as ethanol.

Safe limits (WHO): Adults: max 25g/day (6 teaspoons) • Children: max 12g/day (3 teaspoons)

To put this in perspective: a single can of Coke contains 39g of sugar — already 156% of the daily limit for an adult. One glass of orange juice has 21g. A flavoured yogurt has 15g. Most people consume 70–100g of sugar per day without realising it.

✦ Lenoir et al. (2007) — PLOS ONE: rats chose saccharin (sweet taste) over intravenous cocaine in 94% of trials. The dopamine reward from sweetness exceeded that of one of the most addictive substances known.

Source: Intense Sweetness Surpasses Cocaine Reward, PLOS ONE 2(8): e698

✦ Ahmed et al. (2013) — Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition: sugar meets all four criteria of substance dependence: bingeing, withdrawal, craving, and cross-sensitisation with other drugs.

Source: Sugar Addiction: Pushing the Drug-Sugar Analogy to the Limit

🍷Alcohol

There is no safe amount of alcohol. The WHO, The Lancet, and the Global Burden of Disease Study (2018) all confirmed this: even moderate drinking increases risk of cancer, liver disease, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular damage. Alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen — the same category as asbestos and tobacco.

Alcohol floods the brain with dopamine (up to 360% above baseline for spirits), then depletes it, creating the cycle of craving. It also suppresses GABA receptors and disrupts sleep architecture, even when you feel like it “helps you relax.”

Safe limit: 0 drinks/day. Any amount carries risk. The previous “1 glass of wine is healthy” was debunked by the 2018 Lancet meta-analysis of 28 million people.

✦ GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (2018) — The Lancet: “The level of alcohol consumption that minimises health loss is zero.”

Source: Alcohol Use and Burden for 195 Countries, The Lancet 392(10152)

☕Caffeine

Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors (the chemical that tells you you’re tired), creating artificial alertness. Over time, your brain creates more adenosine receptors to compensate — meaning you need more caffeine just to feel normal. Withdrawal causes headaches, fatigue, irritability, and depression.

Safe limits (EFSA): Adults: max 400mg/day (≈4 cups of coffee) • Pregnant women: max 200mg/day • Children: 3mg/kg body weight

An espresso = 63mg • filter coffee = 95mg • energy drink = 80–160mg • green tea = 28mg • dark chocolate (30g) = 24mg

🍔Ultra-processed foods

Engineered combinations of sugar, salt, fat, and flavour enhancers are designed to override your brain’s satiety signals. The “bliss point” — the precise ratio that maximises craving — is calculated by food scientists to make you eat more than your body needs. These products trigger dopamine responses similar to addictive drugs.

Safe limit: As little as possible. The NOVA classification system identifies them as Group 4 foods. Studies show that every 10% increase in ultra-processed food intake raises all-cause mortality by 14%.

Examples: instant noodles, packaged snacks, fast food burgers, frozen pizzas, breakfast cereals, industrially-made bread, sugary drinks, processed meats (hot dogs, nuggets)

✦ Hall et al. (2019) — Cell Metabolism: in a controlled NIH trial, participants on an ultra-processed diet consumed 500 more calories per day than those eating unprocessed food, despite meals being matched for nutrients.

Source: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake, Cell Metabolism 30(1)

Why you didn’t know

These substances are socially accepted drugs. They are in birthday cakes, business lunches, holiday traditions, and children’s lunchboxes. The food and alcohol industries spend billions on marketing to keep them normalised. Tobacco was once “doctor-recommended” too — until science caught up.

The fact that everyone does it does not mean it is safe. Awareness is the first step to freedom. You don’t have to quit everything overnight. You just have to see it clearly — and then decide for yourself.

⚠ What ultra-processed foods do to your body

• Engineered addiction — UPFs are designed for a “bliss point” of salt, sugar, and fat that overrides your body’s natural fullness signals.

• Microbiome destruction — emulsifiers and preservatives kill beneficial gut bacteria, linked to depression, obesity, and autoimmune disease.

• Nutrient void — high in calories, almost zero in actual nutrition. Your body stays hungry because it never got what it needed.

• Overeating by design — NIH research (2019) showed people eat 500 more calories/day on ultra-processed diets vs. whole food diets, even when matched for nutrients.

• Systemic inflammation — seed oils, artificial colours, and chemical additives trigger immune responses throughout the body.

The science of change

Humans act to prevent pain before they pursue pleasure. Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979) proved that losses are felt approximately twice as strongly as equivalent gains. This is why knowing what these substances do to your body is more powerful than knowing what health could feel like.

But sustained change requires both — start with awareness of the pain, then build toward the positive vision. Your trackers above show you what you are leaving behind, and the goals below show what you are gaining.

✦ Prochaska & DiClemente (1983) — The Transtheoretical Model shows that awareness of negative consequences is the primary driver in the early stages of change, while positive reinforcement sustains it in later stages.

Source: Stages and Processes of Self-Change of Smoking, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 51(3)

Your goal & how to get there
🎯

What you are protecting

Research shows that fear of losing what you love is a stronger motivator than the promise of gaining something new. You are not giving up pleasure — you are protecting the life, the people, and the body that matter most to you.

💔
WHAT YOU LOSE

Energy, sharp thinking, deep sleep, stable mood, healthy skin, strong bones, years with your family

💛
WHAT YOU GAIN

Freedom from cravings, mental clarity, real energy, beautiful aging, being fully present for your loved ones

5 proven strategies to overcome habits
🔬

1. Micro-reduction (Tapering)

Reduce by ¼ of a unit each day. Your brain barely notices the shift, but in 30 days the baseline has moved entirely. This is how pharmacological tapering works — and it works for sugar, caffeine, and alcohol too.

🔁

2. Replacement, not removal

Every craving is a request for dopamine. If you remove the source without replacing the reward, your brain rebels. Swap the source — dates for candy, sparkling water for soda, herbal tea for late-night snacking. The pleasure stays, the damage leaves.

💪

3. Identity-based change

James Clear (Atomic Habits): “Every action is a vote for the person you want to become.” Stop saying “I’m trying to quit sugar” and start saying “I don’t eat processed sugar.” The shift from behaviour to identity is what makes change permanent.

🙋

4. Environment design

Willpower is finite — environment is permanent. Remove triggers: don’t keep sugar in the house, don’t walk past the bar, don’t keep energy drinks in the fridge. Make the right choice the easy choice. B.J. Fogg (Stanford): “Make it invisible, and you won’t have to resist it.”

🤗

5. Self-compassion, not punishment

Dr. Kristin Neff’s research shows that self-compassion after a slip is more effective than self-criticism. Guilt triggers the “what-the-hell effect” (Polivy & Herman, 1985) — after one failure, you abandon the whole effort. Forgive the slip, learn from it, return to the practice. Progress is not perfection.
